lessons.title: Comparing signed numbers and using comparison signs
lessons.summary: Read signed values on a number line and decide when comparison signs include equality.
lessons.objective: Read signed values on a number line and decide when comparison signs include equality.
lessons.before: Read negative whole numbers and decimals. On a horizontal number line, identify zero and point to the right.
lessons.ideas:
Place the numbers on the same scale. A number to the left is smaller. Between two negative numbers, the one further from zero is further left.

The signs \(<\), \(=\) and \(>\) give three distinct comparisons. \(\ne\) is true for unequal values. \(\le\) or \(\ge\) may include the equal case.

Use \(x\le b\) for ‘at most \(b\)’ and \(x\ge b\) for ‘at least \(b\)’. The strict forms exclude the boundary.
lessons.method:
What makes one signed value larger?

Choose one fixed direction before comparing. A value increases as you move to the right, even while you are left of zero.

Which signs make a comparison true?

First decide whether the left value is smaller, equal or larger. Then read the requested sign from left to right.

How do I apply a limit or order a whole list?

Identify the comparison required by the wording. Sort left to right for smallest first, and right to left for largest first.
mistakes: The digit 7 is greater than 2, but the point −7 is further left than the point −2.
Two equal values can satisfy both inclusive comparisons. ‘More than’ excludes equality, and ‘at least’ includes it.
Include a value equal to the limit only when the sign is inclusive.

examples.title: Compare signed whole numbers
examples.question: Choose the correct sign for \(-5\;\square\;-2\).
examples.solution:
Start at zero. Both values lie on its left because they are negative.

The point at \(-5\) is further left than \(-2\).

Reading the pair in the requested order gives \(-5<-2\).

examples.title: Find all true symbols
examples.question:
Which option lists every symbol that makes \(3\;\square\;3\) true?

A. \(<,\ \le,\ e\)   B. \(=,\ \le,\ \ge\)   C. \(>,\ \ge,\ e\)   D. \(=,\ e\)
examples.solution:
The exact comparison is \(3=3\).

Equal values satisfy both inclusive comparisons.

The complete set of true symbols is \(=,\ \le,\ \ge\).

examples.title: Distinguish ‘more than’ from ‘at least’
examples.question: A label says that a carton contains more than 6 items. The possible counts are \(6,\quad 8,\quad 3,\quad 10,\quad 5\). Give all the counts that agree with the label as a set.
examples.solution:
‘More than 6’ means \(n>6\). It excludes \(6\).

Find the supplied points that lie to the right of this boundary.

The possible counts are \(\left\{8,10\right\}\).

lessons.title: Ordering decimals, fractions and measurements
lessons.summary: Compare place-value columns, use equal-sized parts and make units match.
lessons.objective: Compare place-value columns, use equal-sized parts and make units match.
lessons.before: Recognise place-value columns and equivalent fractions. Use a shared length unit for both measurements.
lessons.ideas:
Extend a decimal with trailing zeroes to make the columns easier to read. For example, \(0.47=0.470\) and \(0.437<0.470\).

Use a positive common denominator. Multiply the numerator and denominator of each fraction by the same factor. If one fraction is above halfway and the other is below, use that benchmark.

For centimetres and millimetres use \(1\,\mathrm{cm}=10\,\mathrm{mm}\). For a decimals-only list, keep the decimal forms and compare place-value columns.
lessons.method:
Which decimal digit decides the order?

Compare from the largest place. Look at the first column where the digits differ.

When can I compare the numerators?

A numerator counts pieces. For it to decide which value is larger, each piece must have the same size.

How do I compare measurements fairly?

Compare like quantities on the same scale. Decide which unit will make the comparison exact and convenient.
mistakes: A decimal with more written digits can be the smaller value. Use the place of each digit.
A larger denominator can mean smaller pieces. Comparing just the two denominators does not work in general.
Comparing the written numbers alone can reverse the order when units differ.

examples.title: Compare decimals digit by digit
examples.question: Choose the correct sign for \(1.3\;\square\;1.207\).
examples.solution:
Line up the decimal points. Extend the shorter decimal with zeroes to show the same place-value columns.

Compare \(1.300\) and \(1.207\) from the left. The first differing column is the tenths column.

The comparison is \(1.3>1.207\).

examples.title: Compare fractions using equal-sized parts
examples.question: Choose the correct sign for \(\frac{7}{12}\;\square\;\frac{4}{9}\).
examples.solution:
Make the fraction parts the same size. Use the positive common denominator 36.

\(\frac{7}{12}=\frac{21}{36}\) and \(\frac{4}{9}=\frac{16}{36}\).

Now compare the numerators. The original fractions satisfy \(\frac{7}{12}>\frac{4}{9}\).

examples.title: Compare lengths in the same unit
examples.question: Choose the correct sign for \(3.1\,\mathrm{cm}\;\square\;35\,\mathrm{mm}\).
examples.solution:
These are both lengths. Put them in the same unit before comparing.

Each centimetre has 10 millimetres, so \(3.1\,\mathrm{cm}=31\,\mathrm{mm}\).

Compare 31 mm and 35 mm. This gives \(3.1\,\mathrm{cm}<35\,\mathrm{mm}\).

lessons.title: Ordering fractions, decimals and percentages together
lessons.summary: Find an exact comparison scale, retain ties and write final answers in their original forms.
lessons.objective: Find an exact comparison scale, retain ties and write final answers in their original forms.
lessons.before: Recall how to express a percentage as hundredths and recognise a mixed number as a whole part plus a fraction.
lessons.ideas:
If all values give exact terminating decimals, use decimals for the working. A tie stays a tie when the forms change. Write an equals sign where two original values match.

Retain the whole part when rewriting a positive mixed number. Compare signed values by position, and check the requested direction before writing your answer.

Convert a percentage to hundredths and match denominators if needed. If a limit is ‘at least’, the boundary value qualifies.
lessons.method:
How can different forms share one scale?

Decide on a shared scale before sorting. Equivalent forms name the same point on the number line.

What changes above one or below zero?

A mixed number combines a whole part and a fraction. A negative sign moves a value to the negative side of the scale.

How do I compare close values without losing an exact result?

Choose a positive common denominator when one decimal would need rounding. Keep comparison steps exact.
mistakes: Keep every original entry. Equal numbers can sit next to each other in either order when the list shows equality.
A percent above 100% is greater than one. A minus sign changes the position, not just the label.
Rounding two different numbers to the same value can create an apparent tie.

examples.title: Order fractions, decimals and percentages
examples.question: Put these numbers in order from smallest to largest: \(\frac{4}{20},\quad 17\%,\quad 0.191\). Enter the three values in the stated order.
examples.solution:
Use a single exact comparison scale. The equivalent decimals are \(\frac{4}{20}=0.200\), \(17\%=0.170\), \(0.191\).

Compare digits from the left after aligning decimal points.

Return to the original forms in your final order: \(17\%<0.191<\frac{4}{20}\).

examples.title: Order values above one
examples.question: Put these numbers in order from smallest to largest: \(1\frac{1}{20},\quad 103\%,\quad 1.055\). Enter the three values in the stated order.
examples.solution:
Use a single exact comparison scale. The equivalent decimals are \(1\frac{1}{20}=1.050\), \(103\%=1.030\), \(1.055\).

Compare digits from the left after aligning decimal points.

Return to the original forms in your final order: \(103\%<1\frac{1}{20}<1.055\).

examples.title: Check a cut-off across different forms
examples.question:
A battery indicator passes if it shows at least \(45\%\) of full charge. Which indicators pass?

A \(\frac{11}{25}\); B \(45\%\); C \(0.453\).
examples.solution:
The decimal cut-off is \(0.450\). ‘At least’ includes equality.

Use the same form: A \(0.440\), B \(0.450\), C \(0.453\).

The qualifying indicators are B and C.

questions.title: Order a signed list
questions.prompt_html: Write these values in order from smallest to largest. Fill the four positions in your answer: \(0,\quad -6,\quad 5,\quad -10\).

All negative values are smaller than \(0\), so they go first.

The full order is \(-10<-6<0<5\).
